title: Smart Meter Texas: How to See Your Usage (2026)
h1: Smart Meter Texas: how to see your usage and use it to compare plans
desc: Smart Meter Texas lets you view 15-minute usage data free. Here's how to register with your ESI ID and use the data to pick a cheaper plan.
lede: Smart Meter Texas (SmartMeterTexas.com) is the free, independent portal where Texans in deregulated areas view their smart meter's 15-minute and daily usage data. You register with your ESI ID and meter number, then use that interval data to see when you actually use electricity and calculate whether a time-of-use or free-nights plan would really save you money.
body:
What Smart Meter Texas actually is

Smart Meter Texas is a free website operated on behalf of the state's transmission and distribution utilities (TDUs) — Oncor, CenterPoint Energy, AEP Texas, and Texas-New Mexico Power. It is not run by your retail electricity provider, and it does not sell you a plan. It simply shows the raw usage data your smart meter already records.

If you live in a deregulated area of Texas and your home has a smart meter (nearly all homes in these service areas do), you can see your usage in 15-minute intervals, not just the one number that shows up on your monthly bill.

How to register: what you need

To create an account you need two pieces of information tied to your service address:

  • Your ESI ID — the 17-to-22 digit number that identifies your specific meter and address. It's printed on your electric bill. If you can't find it, our ESI ID lookup guide explains exactly where to look and how to decode it.
  • Your meter number — a separate, shorter number also printed on your bill, usually near the usage summary.

During signup you'll also confirm details like your mailing address or a recent bill amount to prove you're the account holder at that address. Approval is typically fast, though first-time 15-minute interval data can take a day or two to populate after your account is verified.

Renters and movers

The ESI ID stays with the meter and address, not with a person, so if you move, you'll need to register again at your new address using the new ESI ID. If you set up service in a new city, pages like our guides to setting up electricity in Houston and setting up electricity in Dallas cover that process.

What you'll actually see on the portal

Once your account is active, you can pull three levels of detail:

  • Monthly usage — close to what's already on your bill.
  • Daily usage — a bar chart of kWh used each day, useful for spotting which days were unusually high (a heat wave, a house guest, a broken thermostat).
  • 15-minute interval data — the real prize. This is the same data your smart meter sends to your utility, broken into 96 slices per day, so you can see exactly when during the day and night you're using electricity.

You can usually export this interval data to a spreadsheet, which is what makes it useful for comparing plans rather than just browsing a chart.

The real value: using interval data to compare plans

Most people stop at "I used 850 kWh this month." The more useful question is: what percentage of that usage happened during the hours a given plan prices differently? That's the one number generic electricity articles never help you calculate, because they don't have your data. You do, once you're registered.

The break-even method

Every Texas plan publishes an Electricity Facts Label (EFL) with its pricing structure. For a free-nights or time-of-use plan, you can work out the exact share of usage that needs to fall in the cheap window for that plan to beat a flat-rate plan. The formula, using a flat price F and a higher daytime price D with free nights:

Break-even night share = 1 − (F ÷ D)

If your actual night-time usage share (read off your interval data) is higher than this number, the free-nights plan wins. If it's lower, you're better off on flat rate.

Worked example 1: a studio apartment

Say your Smart Meter Texas export shows 600 kWh total for the month, with 150 kWh falling between 9 p.m. and 6 a.m. (25% of usage) and 450 kWh during the day (75%).

Compare two illustrative EFL structures:

  • Plan A, flat rate: 15.94¢/kWh all hours (Texas's current average price) → 600 kWh × $0.1594 = $95.64.
  • Plan B, free nights: $0/kWh from 9 p.m.–6 a.m., 21¢/kWh the rest of the day → 450 kWh × $0.21 = $94.50, plus $0 for the night kWh.

Break-even night share for Plan B = 1 − (15.94 ÷ 21) = 1 − 0.759 = 24.1%. This apartment's actual night share (25%) is just above break-even, so Plan B saves about $1.14 a month — a real but modest edge. Our free-nights plans guide walks through more scenarios where the math tips further one way or the other.

Worked example 2: a large house in summer

Now say a four-bedroom house pulls 2,000 kWh for a summer month, and the interval export shows 500 kWh (25%) falling in the 3–7 p.m. peak window, with the remaining 1,500 kWh (75%) off-peak.

  • Flat plan: 2,000 kWh × $0.1594 = $318.80.
  • Time-of-use plan (illustrative): peak 30¢/kWh, off-peak 12¢/kWh → (500 × $0.30) + (1,500 × $0.12) = $150 + $180 = $330.00.

Break-even peak share for this TOU structure = (F − O) ÷ (P − O) = (15.94 − 12) ÷ (30 − 12) = 3.94 ÷ 18 = 21.9%. This house's actual peak share (25%) is above that break-even, which means the TOU plan costs more, not less. Without pulling the interval data, this household might have signed up for a time-of-use plan expecting savings and ended up paying $11.20 more a month instead.

Side-by-side: how the two examples compare

HouseholdTotal kWhCheap-window shareBreak-even shareFlat costAlt. plan costResult
Studio apartment600 kWh25% (nights)24.1%$95.64$94.50Free-nights plan saves $1.14
Large house2,000 kWh25% (peak)21.9%$318.80$330.00Flat plan saves $11.20

The lesson isn't that one plan type is always better. It's that the same 25% share can mean opposite outcomes depending on which hours the discount or surcharge applies to, and whether your usage actually lines up with it. You only find that out by pulling your own interval data.

Other ways to use your smart meter data

Beyond comparing plans, the interval export is useful for troubleshooting. If you're wondering why your electric bill is so high, daily usage charts can isolate the exact day usage jumped, which narrows down whether it was weather, a new appliance, or a billing error. You can also cross-check your retailer's bill against the TDU's own delivery charges — see our breakdown of Texas TDU delivery charges by utility — since delivery rates update every March 1 and September 1 and are billed separately from your energy charge.

What to do next

This week: find your ESI ID and meter number on a recent bill (or use our lookup tool if you can't locate it), register at Smart Meter Texas, and wait a day or two for interval data to populate. Export a full month, sum your usage into the time windows that matter for any plan you're considering, and run the break-even math above before you switch. If you decide a change makes sense, compare current Texas electricity rates and check whether a fixed or variable rate fits your situation before you sign anything.
faq: Is Smart Meter Texas free to use?
Yes. It's operated for the state's TDUs at no cost to residents in deregulated areas with a smart meter, and it doesn't require you to buy anything.
How do I find my ESI ID to register?
Your ESI ID is printed on your electric bill, usually near the usage or account summary. Our ESI ID lookup guide shows exactly where to find it and what the digits mean.
How current is the 15-minute interval data?
Data generally posts within a day or two of being recorded, though first-time setup can take slightly longer while your account and meter link are verified.
Can I use Smart Meter Texas if I rent my home?
Yes, as long as the electric account and ESI ID are in your name at that address. If you move, you'll need to register again using the new address's ESI ID.
